blocks.x: Towards the end of Zach Cregger’s latest update of the Resident Evil franchise, Austin Abrams, playing a courier who unwittingly stumbles into a zombie apocalypse, has to execute a precision shot with a handgun across a hospital skybridge that has been collapsed by the aforementioned undead to save himself. Bryan narrows his sights and, using the training he’s amassed over the course of Cregger’s fatless, 95-minute horror/thriller/comedy sidequest of a film, snipes a broom barricading a double door, sending an army of brain-thirsty zombies cascading off the edge of the 24th floor, onto a toxified flesh golem blob scaling the building just below, momentarily saving the day. Abrams holds his arms aloft in victory and screams: “Yeaaaahhhh!!!!! Video games! Yeah-HA!”

“Video games! Yeah-HA!” would make a fine alternate title for Cregger’s new movie, the eighth adaptation of Capcom’s Resident Evil, a franchise that has somehow become the standard bearer for video game cinema. It is our longest lasting, highest-grossing game-based series, one now manned by one of the most exciting young American genre directors working today. And what he’s pulled off with this latest installment is, without any qualification, the greatest video game movie ever made.

I’ve alternately enjoyed and struggled with Cregger’s first two major features, Barbarian and Weapons, expertly made classic structures with an iron-grip on tone but a hammy, burdensome way of conveying their thematic preoccupations. Resident Evil, however, has none of this message-mongering, allowing us to revel in virtuosic, button-mashing craft. As a result, this is my favorite of Cregger’s films by a wide margin.

The video game film is now a 30+ year old genre that began with the batshit Bob Hoskins Mario Brothers adaptation in 1993. Cregger has succeeded where his predecessors have failed over and over again because he has little to no interest in mythology or dimensional characterization and instead saves all his imagination and energy for the primal experiential thrill of gameplay mechanics. Cregger junks much of the fan service that has dragged down many of the infamous critical and/or commercial bombs that define the genre, but has made a film that relishes in the gamification of cinematic language: Hyper-spatial awareness, puzzle-solving process, and POV shots that I suspect will appeal to fans in ways merely gesturing towards Easter eggs from past iterations of Resident Evil never have. It’s making a lot of money, too: $60 million domestic and $108 million globally in its opening weekend.

Legitimate competition in the video game movie field has been historically weak. Game adaptations tend to be grubby—poorly directed and acted. It’s a cohort of undercooked cash grabs that suffer from a poverty of technology and ideas and serve as little more than generic vessels that reflect trends in better genre filmmaking as opposed to real, thoughtful expressions of their IP.

Recent improvements to the quality of video game-adapted entertainment have mostly happened on the small screen, with hits like HBO’s The Last of Us and Amazon Prime’s Fallout, as well as with ostensibly family friendly theme-parkified entertainments like Sega’s blockbuster Sonic franchise, Nintendo’s pair of CGI Mario films, and Warner Brothers’ breakout, pomo, alt-comedy Minecraft adaptation. Even films like John Wick or Kane Parsons Portal-inspired Backrooms have repurposed some of the genre’s conventions, and I’d be remiss to leave out this spring’s excellent Japanese import Exit 8, a more ponderous and psychological adaptation of a slower game, without the deep bag of gags, thrills and cheat codes Cregger has uploaded into his Resident Evil.

This is why Cregger’s latest lands as a revelation: at long last, a wildly talented filmmaker at the peak of his powers has focused all his energy on a fine-tuned movie that understands the scary, heart-palpitating fun of a horror-FPS and successfully ports it to the big screen as no other game movie has before.

Whether Resident Evil represents a great leap forward remains to be seen. Cregger, after all, has expressed no interest in returning, though the film’s considerable box office success could tempt him to change his mind. But even if he doesn’t, he’s dramatically recoded what the video game movie is and can be. Video games! Yeah-HA!, indeed.
